class.title: Setting Boundaries in Work Group Chats
class.objective: Say a clear, calm "no" to unwanted comments and personal contact from coworkers, lock down what they can see on your personal accounts, and know when to escalate.
class.northStar: I used to laugh along when the group chat got personal. Now I have one sentence ready, and it takes 10 seconds. Let me show you mine.

block.name: The Hook: "It's Just a Joke"
block.text: April's team uses a group chat to swap shifts. Over a few weeks, a coworker started posting comments about her outfits. Others reacted with laughing emojis. When she didn't reply, he messaged, "Relax, it's just a joke."
Around the same time, her shift manager followed her personal Instagram and started liking old photos from years ago.
April felt she couldn't say anything without being called "too sensitive." But comments about your body or personal life in a work chat aren't part of your job, and you're allowed to stop them.
block.question: Have you ever stayed quiet in a work chat because you didn't want to be "that person"?

block.name: The One Thing
block.text: Today you'll learn to set a boundary in writing, in one short message, and to control who from work can see your personal accounts.
This matters because silence is often read as "okay." A short, calm written boundary makes your "no" clear and creates a record if it keeps happening.

block.name: Core Concept: Clear, Calm, Written
block.text: A good boundary message is short, names the behavior, and says what you want instead. Example: "Please don't comment on my appearance in this chat. Let's keep it to work."
You don't need to explain, apologize, or argue. "It's just a joke" doesn't change whether it's okay. You decide what's okay about your own body and life.
Your personal accounts are yours. You can make them private, remove followers, restrict or block coworkers, and turn off "suggest my account to others" without telling anyone.
If the behavior continues after you've said no, it's no longer a misunderstanding. That's the time to take screenshots and report it to a manager you trust or HR.
block.question: Why is a written boundary in the chat sometimes better than saying it out loud in person?

block.name: Real Examples: Pick the Best Reply
block.text: Situation: A coworker posts "Someone's dressed up today 😏 who's it for?" with your name tagged.
Weak reply: "lol stop." It can be read as playing along.
Strong reply: "Please don't comment on how I look in the work chat. Thanks." It's calm, clear, and on the record.

Situation: Your manager sends a follow request to your private Instagram. You can leave it pending, decline it, or accept and add them to a "Restricted" list. You don't owe anyone access to your personal life.
block.question: Write your own one-sentence boundary for a comment you've seen in a chat. How does it feel to read it out loud?

block.name: Hands-On: Lock Down and Prepare
block.step: Instagram: go to Settings, then Account privacy, and turn on Private account.
Instagram: open your Followers list and remove, restrict, or block anyone from work you don't want there.
Instagram: in Settings, under Accounts Center or "Suggested accounts", turn off suggesting your account to others so coworkers are less likely to find you.
Write your boundary sentence in your notes app so it's ready to copy and paste when you need it.
Mute the work group chat outside work hours if your app allows it.
block.question: Which coworker would you remove or restrict first, and what's stopped you from doing it before?

close.oneAction: Within 24 hours, set your personal Instagram (or another account) to private and review who from work follows you.
close.teachingPrompt: Your friend says, "My coworkers keep joking about my body in the group chat, but I don't want to make it weird." What sentence would you give her to send?
close.resource: Instagram Help Center: privacy, restrict, and block

q.text: A coworker keeps posting comments about your outfits in the team group chat. When you don't reply, he says "it's just a joke." What's true?

option.feedback: Calling it a joke doesn't make it okay if it's unwanted.

q.option: If it's a joke, you have to accept it

option.feedback: Silence is often read as being okay with it.

q.option: You're allowed to tell him to stop, and comments about your body aren't part of your job

option.feedback: Leaving the chat may cut you off from shift updates you need.

q.option: You should leave the chat and miss shift updates

q.text: What makes a strong boundary message?

option.feedback: Long explanations invite arguments.

q.option: A long paragraph explaining all your feelings
Short, names the behavior, and says what you want instead

option.feedback: Apologizing makes it sound like you did something wrong.
An emoji can be read as playing along.

q.option: A laughing emoji so it doesn't seem serious

q.text: Which reply is the clearest boundary?
q.option: "Please don't comment on how I look in the work chat. Thanks."

option.feedback: "lol stop" can be read as playing along.
Insults can escalate things and be used against you.
This doesn't say what you want to stop.

q.text: Why can it help to set your boundary in writing in the chat?

option.feedback: The goal isn't embarrassment. It's clarity.
Writing doesn't guarantee they'll stop, but it helps.
Writing isn't required by law, but it helps you.

q.option: It's clear, it can't be misheard, and it creates a record if it keeps happening

q.text: True or false: you have to explain why a comment bothers you before you can ask someone to stop.

option.feedback: You don't owe anyone a reason to stop commenting on your body or life.

q.text: Your shift manager sends a follow request to your private Instagram. What are your options?

option.feedback: You don't have to accept anyone, even a boss.

q.option: You have to accept because they're your boss

option.feedback: You don't need to delete your account.

q.option: Leave it pending, decline it, or accept and restrict them. It's your choice.

option.feedback: Asking a coworker to decide for you isn't needed.

q.option: Ask the group chat to vote on it

q.text: What does setting your Instagram account to private do?
q.option: Only approved followers can see your posts and stories

option.feedback: Private accounts can still be messaged in some cases.

q.option: It stops anyone from ever messaging you

option.feedback: It doesn't hide you from people who already follow you.

q.option: It removes all your current followers

option.feedback: It doesn't delete anything.

q.text: A coworker is liking years-old photos on your profile. What's a quick way to limit what they see without a confrontation?

option.feedback: Posting about it can escalate things.

q.option: Post a story calling them out

option.feedback: Liking their photos back doesn't set a boundary.
Changing your name doesn't limit their access.

q.option: Remove them as a follower, or restrict or block them

q.text: You set a clear boundary and the comments keep happening. What does that tell you?

option.feedback: After a clear no, it's no longer a misunderstanding.

q.option: It's time to take screenshots and report it to a manager you trust or HR

option.feedback: Repeating yourself forever isn't the only option.

q.option: You should keep asking nicely forever

option.feedback: You didn't cause it by speaking up.

q.option: You made it worse by speaking up

q.text: True or false: "It's just a joke" means the comment is okay.

option.feedback: Whether it's okay depends on whether it's unwanted, not on what it's called.

q.text: A coworker starts private-messaging you late at night about your dating life. What's a good boundary?

option.feedback: Answering keeps the conversation going when you don't want it.

q.option: Answer so he doesn't get upset

option.feedback: Blocking is an option, but if you work together, a clear written no first helps if you need to report later.

q.option: "I'd like to keep our messages about work." Then save a screenshot in case it continues.

option.feedback: Sharing it in the group chat can escalate things.

q.option: Post his messages in the group chat

q.text: What should you do with screenshots of unwanted comments?

option.feedback: Posting them can escalate things and break work rules.

q.option: Save them somewhere private that only you control, with the date

option.feedback: Your employer controls work drives.

q.option: Save them only on a shared work drive

option.feedback: Deleting them loses your proof.

q.option: Delete them so you can move on

q.text: Which of these is a reasonable boundary about work chats?

option.feedback: Shift updates are part of the job.
Threats aren't a boundary.
Being always available isn't a boundary.

q.option: Keeping the work chat about work, and muting it outside work hours

q.text: Turning off "suggest my account to others" on Instagram helps because...
q.option: Coworkers are less likely to find your personal account

option.feedback: It doesn't affect who already follows you.
It doesn't make your posts disappear.
It doesn't change your password.

q.text: Someone replies to your boundary with "Wow, you're so sensitive." What's the best next move?

option.feedback: You don't need to apologize for setting a boundary.
Arguing in the chat rarely helps.

q.option: Don't argue. Your boundary stands. Save a screenshot in case it continues.

option.feedback: Changing yourself isn't the fix.

q.option: Change how you dress so they stop

q.text: Pushback: "If I say something, I'll look like I can't take a joke." What's the best response?

option.feedback: Agreeing keeps you stuck with comments you don't want.

q.option: "One calm sentence isn't overreacting. It just tells people where the line is."

option.feedback: Going straight to anger usually escalates things.
Quitting isn't the first step.

q.text: Pushback: "My boss follows me, so I can't make my account private." What's the best response?

option.feedback: Your personal account isn't part of your job.
You don't need to delete everything.
Posting less doesn't limit who sees what you do post.

q.option: "Your personal account is yours. You can make it private or restrict them without telling them."

q.text: Pushback: "Reporting a group chat is pointless, it's just words." What's the best response?
q.option: "Repeated comments about your body at work can be harassment. Screenshots with dates make it real to HR."

option.feedback: Words can be harassment when they're repeated and unwanted.
Public shaming can backfire.
Waiting for something worse isn't safe.

q.text: Teaching: you have 10 minutes to teach a friend this topic. What should you do first?

option.feedback: Definitions first lose people. Start with something she can do.

q.option: Explain the legal definition of harassment

option.feedback: Stories alone don't give her a tool.

q.option: Tell her about every bad coworker you've had
Help her write her own one-sentence boundary and save it in her notes

option.feedback: Sending a link skips the part where she actually does it.

q.option: Send her a link and leave

q.text: Teaching: your friend sent her boundary, and a coworker kept posting comments anyway. She's upset. What do you tell her?

option.feedback: She didn't fail. He ignored a clear boundary.

q.option: "You did the right thing. Now screenshot it with the date and report it to a manager you trust or HR."

option.feedback: Leaving the chat may cut her off from shifts and doesn't stop him.
Waiting lets it keep going.
